Q221967.title: Brusilov Offensive
Q221967.place: Eastern Front: Volhynia, eastern Galicia and Bukovina (today north-western Ukraine)
paras: The Brusilov Offensive was the great Russian attack on the Eastern Front of the First World War that began on 4 June 1916 and lasted into the autumn (HISTORY says it was shut down on 20 September; Wikipedia says late September). It was led by General Aleksei Brusilov, commander of Russia's South-Western Front, against the armies of Austria-Hungary and, increasingly, Germany, in the region that is now north-western Ukraine. Wikipedia calls it the Russian Empire's greatest feat of arms in the war.

Under the Chantilly agreement of December 1915 the Allies had promised simultaneous offensives in 1916. The Germans were attacking at Verdun, and in May the Austro-Hungarians struck the Italians in South Tyrol (the Trentino), so Italy pressed urgently for a relief offensive in the east. Brusilov insisted on attacking along a broad front rather than at a single point; according to Manfried Rauchensteiner's history of Austria-Hungary in the war, the Russian chief of staff Mikhail Alekseev begged him on the evening of 3 June to postpone and narrow the attack, and Brusilov refused.

The offensive opened with a carefully prepared barrage that tore gaps in the Austro-Hungarian wire and buried defenders in their dugouts, and the infantry then stormed the first lines from close range. Kaledin's 8th Army broke the Austro-Hungarian 4th Army of Archduke Joseph Ferdinand around Lutsk, which the Russians occupied within days; Wikipedia says the 4th Army fell from 117,800 men to 35,000 in four days. Further south the Austro-Hungarian 7th Army was also driven back, and Russian forces went on to take cities including Brody, Kolomyia and Chernivtsi and reach the Carpathian foothills. Austria-Hungary had to halt its Italian offensive, and Germany sent divisions from the west to shore up its ally.

The cost was enormous on both sides, and the figures differ widely. Wikipedia gives 500,000 to 1,000,000 Russian casualties, about 616,000 Austro-Hungarian and 148,000 to 350,000 German, while HISTORY puts Austro-Hungarian losses at 1.5 million, including 400,000 prisoners. The offensive eased pressure on the French at Verdun and on the Italians, inflicted losses on the Austro-Hungarian army from which it never recovered, and brought Romania into the war on the Allied side. But Russia's own losses were so heavy that, as Wikipedia notes, many historians see them as contributing to the collapse of the Russian army and the revolution of 1917.

claims: The Brusilov Offensive began on 4 June 1916 (Wikipedia, Rauchensteiner, HISTORY) and lasted until late September (Wikipedia; HISTORY: shut down on 20 September 1916).

Wikipedia: the Russian Empire's greatest feat of arms during the war.

Under the Chantilly Agreement of December 1915 Russia, France, Britain and Italy committed to simultaneous attacks in summer 1916 (Wikipedia); Germans were storming Verdun and Austria-Hungary attacked in South Tyrol in May 1916; the Italian High Command urgently requested a relief offensive (Rauchensteiner).
Brusilov planned an attack on a broad front; Alekseev doubted the method and on the evening of 3 June asked him to postpone and attack with a narrow spearhead; Brusilov refused (Rauchensteiner).

A barrage of unforeseen strength destroyed wire obstacles and buried defenders in dugouts; Russian storm troops attacking from close range took the first Austro-Hungarian line (Rauchensteiner; Wikipedia: artillery opened breaches, creeping barrage).
Kaledin's 8th Army broke the Austro-Hungarian 4th Army of Archduke Joseph Ferdinand around Lutsk, which the Russians occupied by 7 June (Wikipedia; HISTORY: the 4th Army was broken within two days).
Wikipedia: within four days the 4th Army's strength fell from 117,800 to 35,000.

The Austro-Hungarian 7th Army was driven back (Wikipedia); Russians took Brody, Kolomyia, Chernivtsi and reached the Carpathian foothills (Wikipedia); Conrad had to close down the Trentino offensive and Germany moved divisions from the west (HISTORY).

HISTORY: Austro-Hungarian losses of 1.5 million men including 400,000 prisoners.

It relieved pressure on the French at Verdun and on the Italians, inflicted irreparable losses on the Austro-Hungarian Army, and induced Romania to join the Entente (Wikipedia; HISTORY: Austria-Hungary never again played a significant role).
Wikipedia: many historians contend Russia's casualties contributed significantly to the army's collapse in 1917 / the onset of the Russian Revolution.

Losses: Wikipedia 500,000-1,000,000 Russian, about 616,000 Austro-Hungarian and 148,000-350,000 German (and 1-1.5 million Central Powers losses June-December 1916 from Russian archives); HISTORY 1.5 million Austro-Hungarian including 400,000 prisoners. Start: the event record's 22 May 1916 was the Julian (Old Style) date; it is corrected to 4 June 1916, given by Wikipedia, Rauchensteiner and HISTORY.

Q187152.title: Balfour Declaration
Q187152.place: London (issued by the British government); concerning Palestine, then Ottoman
paras: The Balfour Declaration was a short statement of British policy issued during the First World War. It took the form of a letter dated 2 November 1917 from the foreign secretary, Arthur James Balfour, to Lord Rothschild, conveying on behalf of the government a 'declaration of sympathy with Jewish Zionist aspirations' that the Cabinet had approved, and asking him to pass it to the Zionist Federation. Its single sentence said that the government viewed 'with favour the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people' and would use its best endeavours to bring this about, 'it being clearly understood' that nothing would be done to prejudice 'the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities in Palestine', or the rights and political status of Jews in any other country. The text appeared in the press on 9 November. Palestine was then an Ottoman region; Wikipedia describes its population as an overwhelming Arab majority, mostly Muslim with Christians, and a small Jewish minority.

Britain had been at war with the Ottoman Empire since November 1914. In early 1915 Herbert Samuel, a Jewish member of the Cabinet, circulated a memorandum proposing British support for Zionist aims in Palestine. After David Lloyd George replaced H. H. Asquith as prime minister in December 1916, formal negotiations with the Zionist leadership began: Sir Mark Sykes met them on 7 February 1917, the French diplomat Jules Cambon sent the Zionist envoy Nahum Sokolow a letter of sympathy dated 4 June, and on 19 June Balfour asked Rothschild and Chaim Weizmann to submit a draft.

Drafts were discussed in the War Cabinet in September and October, with submissions from Zionist and non-Zionist Jews but, as Wikipedia notes, no representation of Palestine's Arab population. The leading Jewish opponent was Edwin Montagu, secretary of state for India; the two safeguard clauses were added in early October to meet such objections. President Woodrow Wilson agreed to the release on 6 October (Wikipedia), and the War Cabinet authorised it on 31 October. According to Wikipedia, the ministers expected propaganda benefits among Jews, especially in Russia and America; the Encyclopaedia Judaica also stresses the wish to forestall German approaches to the Zionists and Lloyd George's aim of bringing Palestine under British control.

Reactions differed sharply. Wikipedia describes the declaration as the first public support for Zionism by a major power, which gave the movement new momentum; the Encyclopaedia Judaica records an enthusiastic response among Jewish communities, above all in Russia, and Jews in Palestine kept 2 November as Balfour Day from 1918 until the Second World War. According to Wikipedia, the Muslim and Christian Arabs who made up almost 90% of Palestine's population strongly opposed it; on 3 November 1918 the Muslim-Christian Association handed the military governor, Ronald Storrs, a protest petition signed by more than 100 notables. The Sharif of Mecca and other Arab leaders regarded it as a breach of earlier British promises made in the McMahon–Hussein correspondence. The British government rejected that reading: its White Paper of June 1922 stated that Sir Henry McMahon's letter of 24 October 1915 had excluded Palestine west of the Jordan from the pledge of Arab independence. Among the Allies, the Encyclopaedia Judaica says that Russia, France, Italy and the United States had approved the declaration in advance; Wikipedia dates the first endorsement by a foreign government to 27 December 1917 (Serbia's government in exile), with French and Italian endorsements following in 1918.

British forces took Jerusalem on 9 December 1917. At San Remo on 25 April 1920 the Allied powers assigned Palestine to Britain as a League of Nations mandate, making Britain responsible for putting the declaration into effect. The Mandate for Palestine, dated in London on 24 July 1922, repeated the declaration in its preamble, made Britain responsible for securing the Jewish national home and developing self-governing institutions while safeguarding the civil and religious rights of all inhabitants, and required it to facilitate Jewish immigration without prejudicing the rights and position of the rest of the population; Wikipedia notes that it was formalised in September 1923. In its June 1922 White Paper the British government interpreted the declaration as meaning a national home founded 'in Palestine', not the conversion of Palestine as a whole, with immigration limited by the country's economic capacity. Intercommunal conflict in Mandatory Palestine began in 1920, and in 1939, according to Wikipedia, the British government acknowledged that the wishes and interests of the local population should have been taken into account. Wikipedia regards the declaration as having led indirectly to the emergence of the State of Israel.

Q659745.title: Italian Front
Q659745.place: Border between Italy and Austria-Hungary: the Isonzo, the Karst, the Trentino and the Alps, later the Piave
paras: The Italian front was the theatre of the First World War along the border between the Kingdom of Italy and Austria-Hungary, fought from 1915 to 1918. Although Italy had been allied with Germany and Austria-Hungary, it stayed neutral when the war began in August 1914; relations in the alliance were already strained by Italian claims to Habsburg lands. In the secret Treaty of London of 26 April 1915, Britain, France and Russia promised Italy territory at Austria-Hungary's expense; Wikipedia lists Trento, Trieste, South Tyrol, Istria and northern Dalmatia. Italy declared war on Austria-Hungary on 23 May 1915.

The front ran for hundreds of kilometres from the Adriatic coast along the Karst plateau and the Isonzo (Soča) river up into the Alps; The Past puts its length at almost 400 miles. In the mountains both sides faced avalanches, extreme cold and difficult supply. The main Italian effort was on the Isonzo, aimed at Gorizia and Trieste: twelve battles were fought there between June 1915 and October 1917, beginning on 23 June 1915. Despite superior numbers and material, the Italians made little headway; in August 1916, when Austria-Hungary had to move troops east to face Russia's Brusilov offensive, they took Gorizia in the Sixth Battle. An Austro-Hungarian offensive from the Trentino in May 1916 made early gains before being pushed back. According to The Past, Austria-Hungary fought alone on this front for more than two years, because Germany refused to intervene against Italy until the autumn of 1917.

After the Eleventh Battle of the Isonzo in 1917 (LeMO: 48 Italian divisions and 6,800 guns on a 70-kilometre front) the Austro-Hungarian line was close to collapse. German troops were then sent to help, and on 24 October 1917 Austro-Hungarian and German forces opened the Twelfth Battle of the Isonzo, known as Caporetto, with gas shells and infiltration tactics. Within two weeks they had broken through to the Piave river. Under a new chief of staff, Armando Diaz, the Italians held a line on the Piave and Monte Grappa, reinforced by British and French divisions, and in June 1918 they threw back a major Austro-Hungarian attack across the Piave.

In late October 1918, as Austria-Hungary was breaking apart, the Italian army attacked across the Piave towards Vittorio Veneto. The Austro-Hungarian front collapsed; Wikipedia says 300,000 soldiers surrendered on 3 November, the day Italian troops entered Trento and Trieste. The armistice signed at Villa Giusti near Padua on 3 November took effect on 4 November 1918. Wikipedia gives over 531,000 Italian military dead in the war and about 400,000 Austro-Hungarian dead on the Italian front. The treaties of 1919 and 1920 gave Italy Trento, Trieste, South Tyrol and Istria, while northern Dalmatia, except Zara, went to Yugoslavia.

Q278960.title: Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty
Q278960.place: Moscow (signed by the USSR, the United Kingdom and the United States)
paras: The Partial Test Ban Treaty (also called the Limited Test Ban Treaty) was signed in Moscow on 5 August 1963 by the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and the United States. It banned nuclear weapon tests in the atmosphere, in outer space and under water, but not underground. The Office of the Historian of the US State Department calls it the first arms control agreement of the Cold War, concluded between President John F. Kennedy and the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev.

Public concern had been growing over radioactive fallout from atmospheric tests, especially after the first hydrogen bombs of 1952–53; Wikipedia cites the US Castle Bravo test of 1954, whose fallout sickened Japanese fishermen. The three powers began negotiating a comprehensive test ban in 1958 and observed a voluntary moratorium on testing, but talks stalled over verification: the United States and Britain wanted on-site inspections to tell underground tests from earthquakes, while the Soviet Union saw these as a cover for espionage. After the U-2 incident of 1960 the prospects faded, and both sides resumed testing in 1961–62.

The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962, together with worries about the spread of nuclear weapons to France and China, gave new impetus to an agreement. The breakthrough came when the negotiators gave up a comprehensive ban and left underground tests, which were hard to detect, outside the treaty; the remaining terms were then agreed quickly in Moscow in the summer of 1963, with W. Averell Harriman leading for the United States and Andrei Gromyko for the Soviet Union.

According to Wikipedia, the US Senate approved ratification by 80 votes to 14 on 24 September 1963, and the treaty came into force on 10 October 1963. France and China did not sign and continued atmospheric testing until 1974 and 1980. The State Department's historians judge that the treaty did little to slow the development and spread of nuclear weapons but set a precedent for later agreements such as the Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968; Wikipedia notes that its entry into force coincided with a large fall in radioactive particles in the atmosphere.

Q1773668.title: Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia
paras: On the night of 20–21 August 1968 the Soviet Union led an invasion of Czechoslovakia by forces of the Warsaw Pact to stop the reforms of the 'Prague Spring'. Wikipedia names the Soviet Union, Poland, Bulgaria and Hungary as the invading states and says that East German forces, apart from a few specialists, were ordered not to cross the border at the last moment; the State Department's historians list East German troops among the contingents. According to Wikipedia, about 250,000 troops took part in the operation, code-named Danube, later rising to about 500,000; Romania and Albania refused to take part.

In January 1968 the reformer Alexander Dubček replaced Antonín Novotný as head of the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia. His leadership ended censorship, allowing open public debate, and in April issued a reform programme that stayed within the communist system. Leonid Brezhnev and other Warsaw Pact leaders feared that the reforms would spread to other states of the Eastern Bloc and that Czechoslovakia might drift out of it. Talks at Čierna nad Tisou and a meeting in Bratislava in the summer did not settle the dispute, and Moscow decided to intervene.

The troops had been moved into position under the cover of announced Warsaw Pact exercises, and they quickly took Prague and other cities and the transport and communication links. The Czechoslovak army put up no effective resistance; people protested with signs, placards and graffiti and argued with the soldiers. Wikipedia counts 137 Czechoslovaks killed and 500 seriously wounded during the occupation. Dubček and several colleagues were arrested and taken to Moscow, where all but one of the Czechoslovak delegation signed the 'Moscow Protocol'; they returned to Prague on 27 August.

Dubček remained party leader until he was forced out in April 1969 and replaced by Gustáv Husák, whose 'normalisation' reversed the reforms, restored censorship and purged liberals from the party. Western governments condemned the invasion, as did Romania, China and Albania, but the Soviet Union blocked efforts to pass a condemnation in the UN Security Council. Moscow's claim of a right to intervene where communist rule was threatened became known as the Brezhnev Doctrine. According to the State Department's historians, the invasion delayed détente with the United States by a few years and led President Lyndon B. Johnson to cancel a summit with Brezhnev.

Q482456.title: Fall of Saigon
Q482456.place: Saigon (today Ho Chi Minh City), South Vietnam
paras: Saigon, the capital of South Vietnam, was taken by the forces of North Vietnam and the Viet Cong on 30 April 1975, ending the Vietnam War. The Paris peace agreement of January 1973 had allowed the United States to withdraw its forces, but, as the State Department's historians note, neither Vietnamese side kept to it and the war went on. In March 1975 the North Vietnamese army under General Văn Tiến Dũng opened an offensive in the Central Highlands and took Buôn Ma Thuột; the South Vietnamese army fell back in a disorderly retreat. After an 11-day stand at Xuân Lộc, the last line of defence before Saigon, it withdrew on 20 April, and President Nguyễn Văn Thiệu resigned the next day.

Thiệu's successor, Trần Văn Hương, resigned on 28 April and was replaced by General Dương Văn Minh, who was expected to seek a ceasefire, but Hanoi would not negotiate. The final attack on Saigon began on 29 April with heavy shelling. That morning the United States ordered Operation Frequent Wind: with Tan Son Nhut airport's runways unusable, American helicopters flew Americans and South Vietnamese linked to the government from the Defense Attaché compound and the US embassy to ships of the Seventh Fleet. Crowds tried to climb the embassy walls to reach the helicopters, and on the ships aircraft were pushed into the sea to make room for more. It was the largest helicopter evacuation in history. The US ambassador, Graham Martin, left before 5 a.m. on 30 April, and the last Marines flew out from the embassy that morning; Wikipedia records that about 420 Vietnamese and South Koreans were left behind in the embassy compound.

At 10:24 on 30 April, according to TIME, Minh announced the unconditional surrender of South Vietnam. Around midday North Vietnamese tanks broke through the gates of the Independence (Presidential) Palace, where Minh was waiting, and the Viet Cong flag was raised over it. The government of South Vietnam ceased to exist. On 2 July 1976 Vietnam was formally reunified as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, with its capital at Hanoi, and Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City. The Vietnamese government calls 30 April the day of the liberation of the South and national reunification; many overseas Vietnamese who fled the South call it 'Black April'.

Q76986.title: Belovezh Accords
paras: The Belovezh (Belavezha) Accords were signed on 8 December 1991 at the Viskuli retreat in the Belovezhskaya Pushcha forest in Belarus by the leaders of three Soviet republics: President Boris Yeltsin of Russia, President Leonid Kravchuk of Ukraine and Stanislav Shushkevich, chairman of Belarus's parliament (the State Department's history says simply that they met in Brest). Their agreement founded a Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), and its preamble stated that the Soviet Union had ceased to exist 'as a subject of international law and a geopolitical reality'.

The Soviet Union had been weakening for several years. Under Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms the Communist Party's hold loosened, and nationalist movements grew in the republics; the Baltic republics moved towards independence from 1988, and by the end of 1990 all the union republics had declared their sovereignty. Gorbachev negotiated a new Union Treaty with nine republics in 1991, which would have turned the USSR into a looser union of sovereign states, but its signing was prevented by the failed coup of hard-line officials in August 1991. After the coup Ukraine declared independence on 24 August, and other republics followed; by early December most of them had proclaimed independence, and Ukraine opposed Gorbachev's plan for a confederation.

On 10 December the parliaments of Ukraine and Belarus ratified the agreement and denounced the 1922 treaty that had created the USSR; Russia's parliament did the same on 12 December. On 21 December the leaders of eleven former Soviet republics met in Almaty to confirm the Belovezh agreements and the end of the USSR. Gorbachev resigned as Soviet president on 25 December 1991, and the Soviet flag over the Kremlin was replaced by the Russian tricolour; the next day a chamber of the USSR Supreme Soviet declared that the Soviet Union had ceased to exist as a state. The United States then recognised all twelve of the newly independent republics.

Q133331.title: First Council of Nicaea
paras: The First Council of Nicaea was an assembly of Christian bishops called by the Roman emperor Constantine I to the city of Nicaea in Bithynia (today İznik, Turkey) in 325. It is counted as the first ecumenical council of the Church. Almost all the bishops came from the eastern half of the empire. Their number is uncertain: Wikipedia says at least 200; the Catholic Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius spoke of more than 250 and Athanasius of 318, while modern reconstructions of the surviving lists of signatories give 220 and 218 names.

The council was called to settle a dispute that had begun in Alexandria a few years earlier. The presbyter Arius taught that the Father alone was eternal and that the Son had been begotten or created by the Father and so had a beginning; his bishop, Alexander of Alexandria, held that the Son was eternally begotten. A council of bishops from Egypt and Libya condemned Arius, but he found supporters elsewhere, among them Eusebius of Nicomedia. When Constantine became sole emperor in 324 after defeating Licinius, he wrote to both men urging reconciliation and sent his adviser Hosius of Corduba to Alexandria; when that failed, he summoned a general council. He opened it in person, and Hosius probably presided over the discussions.

The bishops adopted a creed declaring the Son 'of the same substance' (homoousios) as the Father and condemning Arius's teachings. All but two bishops signed it; Arius and the two who refused, Theonas and Secundus, were excommunicated and exiled to Illyria, and Arius's writings were ordered burned. The council also settled how the date of Easter was to be calculated, adopting the practice of Rome and Alexandria rather than relying on the Jewish calendar, dealt with the Melitian schism in Egypt, and issued twenty canons. The sources differ on when it ended: Wikipedia says it closed in the first weeks of July, with the bishops invited to Constantine's celebration of his twentieth year on the throne on 25 July, while the Catholic Encyclopedia dates the end of the sessions to 25 August.

The decision did not end the controversy. According to Wikipedia, Arius's supporters soon regained influence at court: Eustathius of Antioch was exiled in 330 and Athanasius, Alexander's successor at Alexandria, was deposed in 335, and the dispute continued through the rest of the fourth century.
claims: Council of Christian bishops convened by Constantine I at Nicaea in Bithynia (today İznik, Turkey) in 325 (Wikipedia; Catholic Encyclopedia: held in 325, bishops summoned to Nicaea by the emperor).
First ecumenical council (Wikipedia; Catholic Encyclopedia).
Attendance almost entirely from the eastern half of the empire (Wikipedia; Catholic Encyclopedia: Nicaea easily accessible especially to bishops of Asia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Greece and Thrace).

The dispute began in Alexandria between Arius and Bishop Alexander; Arius held that the Father alone was eternal and the Son was created/begotten with a point of origin; Alexander that the Son was eternally generated (Wikipedia; Catholic Encyclopedia: the heresy of Arius, anathema on the view that 'there was a time when He was not').

A council of bishops of Egypt and Libya condemned Arius (Wikipedia; Catholic Encyclopedia: more than one hundred bishops from Egypt and Libya anathematized Arius); Eusebius of Nicomedia supported him (Wikipedia; Catholic Encyclopedia: Arius went to Nicomedia).

Constantine opened the council; Hosius probably presided (Wikipedia: 'may have presided'; Catholic Encyclopedia: Constantine opened the session; the actual president seems to have been Hosius).

Q1348630.title: Ridda Wars
Q1348630.place: Arabian Peninsula (Najd, al-Yamama, Bahrain, Oman, Mahra, Yemen and Hadhramaut)
paras: The Ridda Wars ('wars of apostasy') were the campaigns fought in 632–633 by Abu Bakr, the first caliph, against Arabian tribes that rejected the authority of Medina after the death of the Prophet Muhammad in June 632. Many tribes stopped paying the zakat tax or renounced Islam, and several rebel movements were led by men who claimed to be prophets themselves: notably Tulayha of the Banu Asad and Musaylima of the Banu Hanifa in al-Yamama; in Yemen, another claimant, al-Aswad al-Ansi, had already risen in revolt before Muhammad's death. Wikipedia cautions that the events are hard to reconstruct in detail because the early Arabic accounts are often contradictory and partisan.

Abu Bakr first sent an army under the young Usama ibn Zayd north towards the Byzantine frontier, as Muhammad had planned, while rebels gathered at Dhu al-Qassah, about 30 miles from Medina. With the forces left in the city he drove them back, and after Usama's return defeated them again at Abraq. He then divided his army into eleven corps, each with its own commander and region. The strongest, under Khalid ibn al-Walid, defeated Tulayha at Buzakha and subdued the tribes of Najd. In al-Yamama, Musaylima defeated first Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl and then Shurahbil ibn Hasana, who had attacked before Khalid arrived; Khalid then joined Shurahbil's remnants and, with about 13,000 men, defeated Musaylima, who was killed in the battle (Wikipedia dates it to December 632).

Other corps restored Medina's authority in Bahrain, Oman, Mahra and Yemen. The last major revolt, of the Kinda tribe in Hadhramaut under al-Ash'ath ibn Qays, ended when the Muslim forces took the fortress of al-Nujayr after a siege; al-Ash'ath was sent to Medina and pardoned. By early 633 the peninsula was united under the caliph: TheCollector says the wars were over by March 633, while the lead of Wikipedia's article gives June 633. Freed from the rebellions, Abu Bakr turned his armies against the Sasanian and Byzantine empires, sending Khalid to Iraq, which began the early Muslim conquests. TheCollector notes that the deaths of many men who knew the Qur'an by heart in the fighting at al-Yamama led Abu Bakr to have it written down.

sources.title: The Ridda Wars (632-633 CE): Arabia's Apostasy Wars Explained

Khalid ibn al-Walid commanded the strongest corps, defeated Tulayha at Buzakha and subdued Najd (Wikipedia; TheCollector).

The Kinda revolt in Hadhramaut under al-Ash'ath ibn Qays ended with the siege and capture of al-Nujayr (Nujair) (Wikipedia; TheCollector); al-Ash'ath was sent to Abu Bakr and released after he repented (Wikipedia).

Afterwards Abu Bakr turned to expansion against the Sasanian and Byzantine empires, sending Khalid to Iraq (Wikipedia; TheCollector: armies poised for invasions of the Byzantine and Sasanian empires).

Q603549.title: Battle of Nahavand
paras: The Battle of Nahavand (Nihawand) was fought in 642 in the Zagros region of western Iran between the army of the Rashidun Caliphate, commanded by al-Nu'man ibn Muqarrin, and an army raised by the Sasanian king Yazdegerd III under the general Firuzan. Since their defeat at al-Qadisiyya in 636 the Sasanians had lost Iraq and their capital Ctesiphon, and Yazdegerd had withdrawn to the Iranian plateau, where he assembled a new army.

The sizes of the armies are uncertain. Both sources give the caliphate's army about 30,000 men; Wikipedia gives the Sasanian army as 50,000 to 150,000, mostly farmers and villagers, while TheCollector says sources vary but that up to 150,000 assembled. Firuzan took up a strong defensive position in the hills. Nu'man, unwilling to attack it head on, drew the Persians out by skirmishing and then an orderly withdrawal; when they pursued him onto broken ground, his troops turned and struck them, and the Sasanian army was destroyed. Both Nu'man and Firuzan were killed. Wikipedia notes that the early accounts of the battle differ.

Nahavand ended organised Sasanian resistance and opened the Iranian plateau to the Muslim conquest. According to TheCollector, the victors called it the 'victory of victories' (fath al-futuh). Yazdegerd fled east and tried in vain to raise new forces; he was murdered at Merv in 651, while nobles in Tabaristan, south of the Caspian Sea, held out for about another century.

sources.title: Why Was the 642 CE Battle of Nahavand Called the 'Victory of Victories?'
